title: Trump's Promise Absolutism Narrative Sustained Long-Tail Credibility Risk Across Repeated Review Cycles
description_short: Trump's Promise Absolutism Narrative Sustained Long-Tail Credibility Risk Across Repeated Review Cycles
description_medium: On March 4, 2026, Trump said he had kept all his campaign promises. A tracker of 75 second-term pledges published by PolitiFact showed about 19% marked “Promise Kept,” 45% “In the Works,” and 31% “Stalled”; the rest were listed as compromises or broken. The comparison tests the breadth of Trump’s statement against the tracker’s status categories, which can change as policies develop.
description_long: PBS NewsHour reported on March 4, 2026, that PolitiFact compared Trump’s statement that he had kept all his campaign promises with its second-term Promise Meter. The tracker covered 75 promises: approximately 19% were marked “Promise Kept,” 45% “In the Works,” and 31% “Stalled”; the small remainder were classified as compromises or broken. The ratings were a snapshot, not a final audit: tracker statuses may change as policies are implemented, and PolitiFact said it evaluates measurable outcomes rather than intentions. Reported examples included a partial rather than full change to taxes on Social Security benefits and Trump’s failure, by the stated deadline, to end the Russia–Ukraine war within 24 hours. The report documents a gap between an unqualified claim of completion and a tracker in which most listed pledges were not marked kept. It does not measure how the statement affected public trust or support a claim about long-term credibility costs. Those consequences should not be inferred from the tracker alone.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Promise Absolutism Narrative Sustained Long-Tail Credibility Risk Across Repeated Review Cycles
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Promise Absolutism Narrative Sustained Long-Tail Credibility Risk Across Repeated Review Cycles

notes: The tracker supports comparison with Trump’s statement; it does not establish the long-term credibility effects asserted in the original title.

title: Trump: Middle East attacks intensify as Trump says he rejects Iran’s attempt to talk
description_short: Trump: Middle East attacks intensify as Trump says he rejects Iran’s attempt to talk
description_medium: As U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran intensified on March 3, Trump said Tehran had sought talks and that he had rejected them as “Too Late!” Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva denied that Tehran had approached Washington. Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that the “hardest hits are yet to come” as Iranian attacks spread across the Gulf.
description_long: The Guardian reported that U.S. and Israeli forces intensified attacks on Iran on March 3, striking command facilities, government sites and missile-launch locations. Trump said on Truth Social that Iran wanted to talk and that he had rejected the approach as too late; he also said the United States could continue the war beyond four or five weeks. Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva denied that Tehran had approached the United States for negotiations, so the claimed overture was disputed in the report. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the “hardest hits are yet to come,” while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth raised the possibility of U.S. troops on the ground. Iran launched missile and drone attacks across the Gulf, including against U.S. bases, embassies and civilian infrastructure. The article reported hundreds of deaths in Iran, citing the Red Crescent’s figure of 787, and described damage to energy and transport sites and sharply rising energy prices. It also noted that U.S. officials gave varying explanations for the war, including preventing a nuclear weapon and changing Iran’s leadership. The report captures escalation and contested diplomatic claims, not proof that negotiations had formally begun.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Middle East attacks intensify as Trump says he rejects Iran’s attempt to talk
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Middle East attacks intensify as Trump says he rejects Iran’s attempt to talk

notes: Iran’s UN ambassador denied that Tehran had sought negotiations; the report attributes the approach claim to Trump.

title: Trump administration warns tariff refund process ‘will take time’
description_short: Trump administration warns tariff refund process ‘will take time’
description_medium: After the Supreme Court invalidated most of Trump’s country-specific tariffs under the 1977 emergency-powers law, the Justice Department told a court that refunds would take time. Companies including FedEx and hundreds of other importers sought repayment. DOJ did not ask the justices to rehear the case, despite Trump’s public complaint and suggestion of a rehearing.
description_long: The Guardian reported that the Justice Department told a court that returning tariffs invalidated by the Supreme Court would take time. Businesses including FedEx had sought reimbursement, and hundreds of companies had filed claims before the ruling in anticipation of it. The Court held that the 1977 law addressing national emergencies did not authorize most of the administration’s country-specific tariffs. DOJ did not ask the justices to rehear the case, even after Trump publicly questioned whether rehearing was possible and argued that refunds would create an undeserved windfall for countries and companies. The article did not give a final refund schedule or say that every importer would qualify; the process remained subject to claims and court proceedings. Trump also criticized the ruling and threatened to impose replacement tariffs in a “much more powerful and obnoxious way,” while officials considered other legal authorities. The report therefore describes the administration’s response to a court ruling and an unresolved reimbursement process. It does not establish the eventual amount paid, the timing of individual refunds or the outcome of each importer’s claim.

preserved_fields.title: Trump administration warns tariff refund process ‘will take time’
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump administration warns tariff refund process ‘will take time’

notes: The linked report gives no comprehensive refund schedule, eligibility determination or final total.

title: Trump: Maine university pulls support from conference on Palestine, citing Trump sanctions
description_short: Trump: Maine university pulls support from conference on Palestine, citing Trump sanctions
description_medium: The University of Southern Maine withdrew access to an on-campus venue shortly before a Palestine conference that included remote participation by Francesca Albanese, a U.N. rapporteur sanctioned by the Trump administration. The university cited federal sanctions law. Organizers searched for another site, while published Treasury guidance said Albanese could participate remotely without prior authorization when no payment or other prohibited service was involved.
description_long: The Guardian reported that the University of Southern Maine revoked an on-campus venue days before the “Consequences of Palestine” conference, citing the planned remote participation of Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories. The Trump administration had sanctioned Albanese the previous July. More than 300 people had registered, and organizers said they were looking for another venue after the university withdrew support. A university system official argued that hosting an event promoted as including a sanctioned speaker could violate federal law. However, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control had issued guidance in December stating that remote participation by Albanese without payment, training or assistance did not require prior authorization. Organizers offered to remove her from the program, but said the university then cited insufficient time to assess the event’s risk. A sociology professor involved in the conference said administrators had raised concerns about possible federal funding cuts; the university denied that it acted in response to political pressure and said it had ended its contract before receiving a letter from Republican lawmakers. The report documents a local venue decision and competing legal explanations. It does not show that Trump personally directed the university’s action or establish what happened to the conference afterward.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Maine university pulls support from conference on Palestine, citing Trump sanctions
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Maine university pulls support from conference on Palestine, citing Trump sanctions

notes: The report describes the university’s decision and the organizers’ response; it does not establish that Trump ordered the venue withdrawal or document the conference’s eventual outcome.

title: Federal Court Jurisdiction Stripping - Supreme Court Power Elimination Through Congressional Action
description_short: Federal Court Jurisdiction Stripping - Supreme Court Power Elimination Through Congressional Action
description_medium: The entry alleges that Congress enacted limits on federal courts’ review of disputes involving immigration, abortion, voting rights and civil liberties. The supplied materials identify no bill, vote or enacted statute supporting that account. They point to a broader legal debate over jurisdiction stripping, but do not establish that judicial review of these claims was eliminated nationwide.
description_long: Congressional power to define some limits on federal court jurisdiction is the subject of an ongoing legal debate, including disputes about how far such limits may reach when constitutional rights are at stake. This entry describes a much more specific event: that Congress passed a law barring federal judges from reviewing executive decisions across immigration, abortion, voting and civil-liberties cases. The materials supplied with the entry do not identify the legislation, its text, a vote, an enactment date or a court decision applying it. Without those details, the claim that Congress removed judicial oversight across these areas cannot be confirmed, and the accompanying assertions that courts became powerless or that the separation of powers was effectively ended are unsupported. The item can be made accurate by identifying the particular proposal or enacted measure and describing its actual scope and legal effect. Until then, it should be understood as an unverified claim about jurisdiction stripping rather than a confirmed nationwide change to the federal courts.

preserved_fields.title: Federal Court Jurisdiction Stripping - Supreme Court Power Elimination Through Congressional Action
preserved_fields.description_short: Federal Court Jurisdiction Stripping - Supreme Court Power Elimination Through Congressional Action

notes: Missing context: no specific enacted bill, text, vote, or implementing court order is identified. Proposed correction: reframe this as a discussion of jurisdiction-stripping proposals and identify any measure before claiming Congress removed judicial review nationwide.

title: Online Privacy Technology Ban - Age Verification Surveillance and Digital Identity Exposure
description_short: Online Privacy Technology Ban - Age Verification Surveillance and Digital Identity Exposure
description_medium: In Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, the Supreme Court voted 6–3 to uphold Texas H.B. 1181, which requires age verification for visitors to covered adult-content websites. Justice Clarence Thomas wrote that states may verify ages to protect minors; Justice Elena Kagan dissented over adults’ access to protected speech. The Internet Society warned that verification can expose sensitive identity and browsing data.
description_long: In Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, the Supreme Court upheld Texas H.B. 1181, a law requiring age verification for people who visit covered websites with sexually explicit content. Justice Clarence Thomas’s majority opinion said the state could use age checks to protect minors; Justice Elena Kagan dissented, emphasizing the burden on adults seeking protected speech. The ruling addressed the Texas statute before the Court. It did not create a federal age-verification mandate, prohibit anonymous internet use across all services or establish that states can track every user’s browsing. The Internet Society argued that common verification methods can connect a person’s identity with sensitive online activity and create privacy and security risks, including exposure if collected data are mishandled or breached. Those concerns describe possible consequences of verification systems; the case record summarized here does not show that Texas created a permanent government database of users’ browsing histories. The decision leaves the law in force and signals that this particular age-verification requirement survived the constitutional challenge. Claims about other states, broader online platforms or government surveillance require separate evidence.

preserved_fields.title: Online Privacy Technology Ban - Age Verification Surveillance and Digital Identity Exposure
preserved_fields.description_short: Online Privacy Technology Ban - Age Verification Surveillance and Digital Identity Exposure

notes: The ruling concerned Texas H.B. 1181. The title’s broader “ban” framing and claims of permanent or nationwide surveillance are not established by the supplied case summary.

title: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds
description_short: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds
description_medium: An Economist/YouGov poll conducted February 27–March 2, 2026, found that 50% somewhat or strongly supported abolishing ICE, while 39% opposed it. Support reached 77% among Democrats and 52% among independents; 68% of Republicans opposed abolition. The Guardian placed the results amid debate over the administration’s immigration enforcement and a partial Homeland Security shutdown.
description_long: An Economist/YouGov poll conducted February 27 through March 2, 2026, found that 50% of Americans somewhat or strongly supported abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, while 39% opposed it. YouGov said this was the first time support in its polling reached 50%. Support included 77% of Democrats and 52% of independents; 68% of Republicans opposed abolition, while 23% supported it. The Guardian placed the result amid the Trump administration’s enforcement operations and a partial Homeland Security shutdown. The YouGov report also found that 75% favored requiring ICE officers to wear identifying uniforms and 59% opposed allowing agents to hide their faces with masks. It reported that 58% said ICE used excessive force and 44% said they had no confidence in the agency. These results show that the poll measured views on agency abolition alongside specific enforcement practices and confidence in ICE. The Guardian connected the polling to scrutiny of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem following the Minneapolis deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. The accessible YouGov article provides response breakdowns but not the sample size or full questionnaire and methodology, so those details remain unavailable.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Half of Americans back abolishing ICE amid Trump crackdown, poll finds

notes: The available YouGov page does not supply the sample size or full questionnaire and methodology.

title: Trump's Own Prewar Intelligence Said the Iran War Wasn't Likely to Change the Regime
description_short: Trump's Own Prewar Intelligence Said the Iran War Wasn't Likely to Change the Regime
description_medium: The linked report’s headline says a prewar U.S. intelligence assessment found that intervention in Iran was unlikely to change its leadership. The supplied material does not identify the assessment, quote Trump’s statements or establish that he publicly promised regime change as a stated war aim.
description_long: A report about a prewar U.S. intelligence assessment is summarized as finding that military intervention in Iran was unlikely to change the country’s leadership. That judgment could be relevant to evaluating claims about the war’s aims, but the supplied account does not identify when the assessment was made, which agency prepared it, how confident analysts were or whether it addressed the same outcome Trump discussed publicly. It also provides no direct quotation or date for Trump’s statements. The evidence here therefore does not establish that he knew a particular assessment contradicted a promise he had made, or that he misrepresented intelligence. A reliable account of the assessment and the specific public remarks would be needed before making that comparison. The headline’s attribution to Trump’s intelligence does not, by itself, show that the assessment was suppressed or used as a pretext for war.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Own Prewar Intelligence Said the Iran War Wasn't Likely to Change the Regime
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Own Prewar Intelligence Said the Iran War Wasn't Likely to Change the Regime

notes: Missing context: the AP page returned HTTP 403; the available headline supplies only the assessment’s broad finding. Needed: assessment date, agency, confidence level, exact scope and Trump’s statements with dates. Proposed correction: describe only the reported intelligence judgment until those particulars can be established.
